title: Kyoto Temple Bans Visitors in Kimonos
paragraphs: For tourists in Japan, dressing up in a kimono and having photos taken can be a memorable part of their trip.

But at one historic temple in Kyoto, problems with visitors wearing kimonos have led to an unusual new rule. Though it's not really the kimonos that are the problem — it's what tourists do while wearing them.

Seirai-in is a 600-year-old temple known for its beautiful rock garden and for its main hall, where a huge painting of a white dragon covers the ceiling. Visitors are encouraged to lie on the floor for a better view of the dragon above them.
In July, however, Seirai-in announced that visitors wearing kimonos or other traditional Japanese clothing were banned from entering the temple.
There are many kimono rental shops in Kyoto's historic areas, and it's common to see tourists dressed in traditional clothing having their photos taken around the city.
But Seirai-in said it was having problems with people in kimonos having elaborate photo sessions in the temple.
According to the temple, some visitors walked onto the carefully raked white sand in the rock garden to pose for photos. Other visitors moved sliding doors to include them in photos and damaged them.
And in one case, someone even started a calligraphy performance in the main hall without permission, and got black ink on the floor.
As well as causing problems for the temple, these photo sessions have been disturbing other visitors who want to pray, see the temple's art, or just enjoy the peaceful surroundings.

Seirai-in is a sub-temple of the larger Kenninji Temple. On its website, Kenninji reminds people that it isn't a photo studio or theme park. It says that visitors who don't follow the rules or behave inappropriately may be asked to leave.
Seirai-in's new rule is a reminder that this 600-year-old temple is a place to be respected, not just a place for photos.
